description: We are TerraPulse, a student team interested in data science, AI, Earth observation, and satellite technology. For the Dancing with the SARs challenge, we are excited to explore SAR data and turn Earth observation data into meaningful insights and visualizations. We are interested in collaborating with people passionate about Earth science, data analysis, AI/ML, coding, and visualization.
summary:
Under the Clouds is an interactive Earth-observation research platform developed by Team Terrapulse for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the Dancing with the SARs challenge.

Using NASA–ISRO NISAR Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery, our project investigates flood-related surface changes in Pakistan, even when cloud cover limits optical satellite observations.

Our Jatoi analysis identified 290 exploratory radar-change clusters covering approximately 0.568 km². We developed an interactive map, a satellite observation calendar, and evidence-based visualizations. We also examined Sentinel-2 imagery, Copernicus Global Flood Monitoring, and JRC historical water information to assess uncertainty.

We evaluated radar screening and exploratory machine learning methods. A separate Dera Ghazi Khan investigation examined 36,841 valid 20 m cells across nine sites and identified 240 radar-change candidates, but independent flood validation remained inconclusive.

Our platform makes satellite observations more accessible while distinguishing potential environmental changes from verified flooding. It is a research prototype, not an operational flood-warning system.
details:
Under the Clouds — Project Details

1. The Problem

Flooding is one of Pakistan's most destructive natural disasters, affecting communities, agriculture, infrastructure, and livelihoods.

During the monsoon season, thick cloud cover can obstruct traditional optical satellite imagery, making it difficult to observe conditions during periods of heavy rainfall and possible flooding.

Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites can collect observations through clouds and in darkness. However, interpreting SAR imagery is challenging because changes in radar backscatter can result from multiple factors, including surface water, soil moisture, vegetation, agricultural activity, and changes in surface roughness.

Our challenge was to explore how NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations could support transparent investigation of possible flood-related surface changes without confusing radar signals with confirmed flooding.

2. Our Solution

Under the Clouds is an interactive geospatial research platform developed by Team Terrapulse for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

The platform combines NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations, satellite-derived comparison data, exploratory machine learning, and interactive mapping to investigate environmental changes in Pakistan.

Our solution includes:

  • Interactive geographical visualization of radar-change candidates.
  • Satellite observation availability information through a Blind Days calendar.
  • Exploratory radar backscatter analysis using HH and HV polarization.
  • Independent satellite-observation checks using Sentinel-2 and Copernicus Global Flood Monitoring.
  • Historical surface-water screening using JRC Global Surface Water.
  • Transparent reports documenting methodology, limitations, and uncertainty.
  • A bilingual, publicly accessible research interface.

Rather than automatically labeling every radar change as flooding, the platform helps users distinguish between observed environmental change and independently verified inundation.

3. How Our System Works

Step 1 — Satellite Data Acquisition

Our research uses NASA–ISRO NISAR Synthetic Aperture Radar observations accessed through NASA's Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF).

We investigate selected radar acquisitions covering locations in Punjab, Pakistan.

We also use complementary Earth-observation information from Sentinel-2, Copernicus Global Flood Monitoring, and JRC Global Surface Water.

Step 2 — Geospatial Preprocessing

We process and analyze radar observations using Python and geospatial libraries.

Our workflow includes geographical alignment, invalid-pixel screening, radar backscatter analysis, and measurement-unit verification.

In corrected-scale experiments, NISAR linear radar power is converted into decibels using:

[
HH_{dB}=10\log_{10}(HH_{linear})
]

This conversion is necessary to interpret radar intensities with appropriate thresholds.

Our research also documented a calibration issue affecting some earlier exploratory experiments, distinguishing those from analyses whose source-code conversion was verified.

Step 3 — Jatoi Surface-Change Analysis

We developed an exploratory radar-change analysis for Jatoi, Punjab, Pakistan.

Our original interactive analysis identified:

  • 290 radar-change clusters
  • 5,679 candidate 10 m pixels
  • Approximately 0.568 km² of candidate surface changes

These results represent areas exhibiting radar-change patterns, not confirmed flooded locations.

A separate focused Jatoi experiment identified 125 exploratory clusters. This experiment used a different study footprint and must not be combined with the original 290-cluster map.

Step 4 — Satellite Evidence and Validation

We investigated the radar candidates using independent satellite-derived observations.

These included:

  • Copernicus Global Flood Monitoring reference estimates.
  • Sentinel-2 optical observations and water-related spectral indices.
  • JRC Global Surface Water historical occurrence information.

In a focused Jatoi optical cross-check, ten selected research locations were examined. Some showed water-like optical signals, but newly occurring inundation was not independently established.

These checks demonstrated the importance of acquisition timing, changing surface conditions, and separating satellite-reference agreement from verified ground truth.

Step 5 — Exploratory Machine Learning

We investigated whether additional radar and spatial features could improve agreement with satellite-derived flood-reference information.

The research compared simple HH backscatter screening against logistic regression approaches, including a six-feature model.

In a geographically separated evaluation experiment within the Jatoi study region, the six-feature model achieved approximately:

  • 48.07% precision-like agreement
  • 86.25% recall-like agreement

These values measure agreement with a satellite-derived reference under the tested conditions. They are not independently confirmed flood-detection precision or recall, and they do not establish generalization to new flood events.

The experiment also suggested that simpler radar-screening approaches can perform comparably to more complex models in the evaluated setting.

Step 6 — Independent-Region Investigation: Dera Ghazi Khan

To investigate how our approach behaves in another geographical region, we conducted an exploratory study in Dera Ghazi Khan using actual NASA–ISRO NISAR acquisitions from 25 June and 19 July 2026.

The two acquisitions had the same radar track, frame, and acquisition mode, enabling a consistent radiometric-screening investigation.

We analyzed nine predefined geographical research sites using native 10 m radar pixels aggregated to 20 m.

Results:

  • 9 research locations examined.
  • 36,841 common-valid 20 m cells.
  • 240 radar-change candidate cells identified using fixed HH screening thresholds.
  • Approximately 0.096 km² of candidate radar changes across the sampled sites.

We also examined 126 Sentinel-2 local observation records and 13 Sentinel-1 catalogue scene records.

However, exact flood-affected settlement locations were not verified, and an appropriate date-matched inundation reference was unavailable. The historical-water exclusion stage was also not applied to this diagnostic.

The July 19 observation may have occurred after floodwater from the earlier July event had receded.

Therefore, this independent-region investigation remains inconclusive. It does not demonstrate verified flooding or establish external-event detection accuracy.

Our detailed methodology, pre-registered evaluation protocol, and research limitations are documented in the project's public GitHub repository.

Step 7 — Interactive Visualization

Our public-facing web application presents radar-change information through an interactive geographical interface.

It allows users to explore candidate locations, examine research evidence, and understand the differences between radar observations and verified flooding.

We also developed a Blind Days calendar showing optical satellite observation availability.

Across a preliminary 150-day calendar:

  • 56 days were classified as optically usable.
  • 12 days were classified as obstructed.
  • 82 days had no Sentinel-2 observation.

Days without satellite images are not automatically treated as cloudy days.

4. Technologies and Tools

Our research and development used:

  • NASA–ISRO NISAR satellite observations.
  • NASA Alaska Satellite Facility data services.
  • Python and Google Colab.
  • NumPy and Pandas.
  • Rasterio and HDF5 processing tools.
  • Scikit-learn for exploratory machine learning.
  • Matplotlib for data visualization.
  • Google Earth Engine.
  • Copernicus Global Flood Monitoring.
  • Sentinel-2 imagery.
  • JRC Global Surface Water.
  • HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Leaflet.
  • GitHub and GitHub Pages for open research documentation and public access.

5. What Makes Our Project Innovative?

Under the Clouds combines radar-based environmental analysis with uncertainty-aware visualization.

Our project focuses on five aspects:

Cloud-independent observations: NISAR radar data allows surface conditions to be investigated when optical observations are limited by cloud cover.

Evidence transparency: The platform distinguishes radar-change candidates from confirmed flooding and communicates the limitations of satellite comparisons.

Accessible research visualization: Interactive maps and a bilingual interface make complex Earth-observation information easier to explore.

Reproducible scientific investigation: The project documents calibration checks, processing assumptions, evaluation limitations, and exploratory results.

Model-complexity comparison: Our machine learning experiments investigate whether additional features meaningfully improve satellite-reference agreement compared with simpler radar screening.

An important part of our innovation is not simply detecting change, but communicating how much confidence can reasonably be placed in an observation.

6. Intended Users and Impact

The intended users of Under the Clouds include:

  • Disaster management organizations.
  • Emergency responders.
  • Agricultural and environmental researchers.
  • Local governments and planning authorities.
  • Students and satellite-data researchers.
  • Communities vulnerable to flooding.

The platform could support environmental-change investigations, research into flood-prone areas, selection of locations for additional verification, and public understanding of satellite observations.

Our longer-term objective is to develop more reliable, accessible, and appropriately validated environmental-monitoring tools for communities exposed to flooding.

7. Scientific Limitations

Under the Clouds is a research prototype, not an operational flood detection or emergency-warning system.

Our scientific limitations include:

  • Radar backscatter changes can result from factors other than flooding.
  • Satellite-derived flood estimates are not equivalent to field-verified ground truth.
  • Satellite acquisition timing may miss short-duration flash floods.
  • Some early exploratory experiments contained calibration uncertainties.
  • The geographically separated Jatoi evaluation does not establish independent-event model generalization.
  • The Dera Ghazi Khan experiment did not establish verified flood labels and did not complete the historical-water exclusion stage.
  • Confirmed inundation area, agricultural damage, and operational flood-detection accuracy have not been demonstrated.

We document these limitations to support responsible interpretation and reproducibility.

8. Future Improvements

Our future development priorities include obtaining better time-matched inundation references, collecting verified ground observations, testing additional flood events, and strengthening the reproducibility of satellite processing.

We also plan to improve uncertainty visualization, explore acquisition-mode comparability where appropriate, and develop more accessible analytical tools for environmental researchers and disaster management organizations.

9. Conclusion

Under the Clouds demonstrates how NASA–ISRO NISAR Synthetic Aperture Radar observations can be combined with geospatial analysis, exploratory machine learning, and interactive visualization to investigate environmental surface changes in Pakistan.

Our project produced a public research platform, exploratory Jatoi radar-change maps, satellite evidence comparisons, and an independent-region diagnostic in Dera Ghazi Khan.

The research highlights a central scientific principle:

Satellite radar can reveal where surface conditions changed, but reliable flood identification requires appropriate, independent evidence.

By making our methodology, limitations, and results accessible, Team Terrapulse aims to contribute to more transparent and responsible satellite-based environmental monitoring.
